issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are strongly social-evaluative and interpersonal (avoiding evaluation, avoiding conflict, rehearsing conversations), which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which contains no social threat, shame, or interpersonal trauma content to explain these strategies.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, the strongest pathway is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies. However, the selected negative appraisals focus on global identity change, chronic misery, and self-blame for being in the situation, while the selected strategies are specifically about managing social scrutiny and interpersonal interactions. That is a weak clinical fit: the strategies do not plausibly follow from the appraisals provided.

issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Memory and appraisals are only partly coherent: terror on recall and olfactory recall fit disaster trauma, but rage on recall is less well supported by the rest of the profile because there is no accompanying appraisal about betrayal, preventability by others, or injustice that would explain intense anger as a central recall response.

For a natural-disaster trauma, intense rage specifically on recall is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on terror, misery, self-change, and generalized avoidance rather than anger at a person or agent. Rage can occur, but here it lacks support from the other selected items and is the least coherent memory item.

'Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation' implies preventable personal failure in getting into the trauma. With a natural disaster, this appraisal is difficult to justify unless there was a very specific risky decision context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. The other appraisals focus on post-trauma change and unhappiness, making this item the clearest mismatch.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, strong self-blame framed as 'the event happened because of the way I acted' is hard to justify clinically unless the disaster involved a very specific preventable action by the patient. In the absence of any such context, this appraisal is implausible for the indexed trauma.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are predominantly interpersonal/social-safety behaviors (avoiding conflict, rehearsing conversations) that fit social threat or shame-based trauma formulations more than a natural disaster PTSD presentation. They do not connect well to the memory/appraisal content provided.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile includes active hypervigilant threat-monitoring ('constantly scan environment for signs of threat') and a global danger appraisal, but the formulation specifies Threat as effectively inactive, with no active links involving Threat and no active Trigger pathways. For a natural-disaster case, these items imply an ongoing threat-focused maintenance pattern that is not supported by the stated formulation.

issues.item: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
issues.explanation: This is not just a weak-edge issue: both items explicitly center current external danger/threat, whereas the active formulation is concentrated on Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory and Negative Appraisals ↔ Maladaptive Strategies without Threat involvement. The remaining items fit a self-focused/post-traumatic change formulation, making these threat-focused items the main incoherent elements.

vignette:
Caleb was nineteen, a fast-food worker who had been on the fry station at a chain restaurant two years ago when the tornado hit. He remembered the way the light turned greenish through the window, then the sound—a freight train roar that seemed to come from inside his own skull. He had dropped the basket of fries and run for the walk-in cooler, wedging himself between boxes of frozen patties as the roof tore away. What stayed with him most was the smell: wet insulation, natural gas, and something metallic that he could still summon without warning when a customer dropped a metal tray or when the fryer oil got too hot. Those smells brought the terror back whole, not just the memory but the actual body panic—his heart slamming, his palms slick—as if he were still crouched in that cooler waiting to die. The images came too, mostly in fragments: the ceiling peeling back, a soda machine toppling, the assistant manager’s face streaked with blood.

Caleb had come to believe that he was permanently changed for the worse, that the person he used to be—the easygoing kid who laughed easily and never worried—was gone. He told his therapist that he used to be happy, but now he was always miserable, and that misery felt like proof that something inside him had broken for good. This sense of permanent damage coloured everything. When he thought about the tornado, he didn’t just remember the fear; he remembered it as confirmation that he was now a defective person, someone who would never feel safe again. And the memories themselves seemed to get worse the more he believed that, as if his negative view of himself made the terror more vivid, more real. He would catch a whiff of something—damp cardboard, propane—and the visual images would flood in, bringing with them the same conviction: *This is who you are now. You’ll never be the same.*

To manage the constant feeling of being broken, Caleb had developed a set of strategies that he hoped would keep things manageable. He rehearsed conversations in his head before any interaction, even a simple order at the drive-through, because he was terrified of saying something wrong and then having to deal with the stress of a conflict. He avoided anything that could be stressful: he turned down extra shifts, stopped seeing friends, stopped calling his mother because he didn’t want to explain why he sounded so flat. And he tried hard not to think about the tornado—he would push the images away, change the channel in his mind, keep himself busy. But these strategies only reinforced his sense of being unrecognisable. The more he rehearsed conversations, the more he felt like an imposter, someone who had to script his own life. The more he avoided stressors, the more he felt incapable of handling normal life. And the more he suppressed the memories, the more they seemed to burst through at unexpected moments, each time confirming that he was beyond repair.

At work, the triggers were constant. The smell of the fryer oil could become, in an instant, the smell of the cooler. A sudden loud noise—a dropped tray, a slammed door—would send him into hypervigilance. He would freeze, rehearsing his next line in his head, telling himself not to react, not to show fear. His manager had noticed that Caleb was jumpy and withdrawn, and had suggested he take a few days off. Caleb had agreed, but the days at home were worse: nothing to distract him, the memories pressing in, the rehearsals turning into obsessive loops. He had started to believe that he would never be able to hold down a job, never have a relationship, never be the person he used to be. That belief was what finally drove him to the clinic—not the memories themselves, but the certainty that he had lost himself, and that suppressing, avoiding, and rehearsing were all he had left, and they weren’t working. He was afraid that therapy would confirm his worst fear: that the damage was permanent. But he was also afraid of staying where he was.
